screens.title: What is a Kanban board?
screens.narratorSegment: A Kanban board is a visual management tool that represents your workflow as a series of stages and the work items that move through them. At its core it makes all work visible, turning hidden tasks into tangible cards that anyone can inspect. This visibility reduces miscommunication about ownership and status and helps teams find where flow is obstructed. Think of it as a communal workspace: cards represent units of work such as user stories, bugs, or tasks, and columns represent the stages those items pass through. The key difference from a simple to-do list is the explicit flow — cards move left to right and the team can apply policies about when they may move. A common misconception is that a board is only a status report; in practice a healthy board is a live artifact that teams pull from, negotiate, and update often. As an example, imagine an e-commerce project where checkout integration waits on A P I keys; by placing a card in a 'Blocked' column the team makes that dependency visible so it can be prioritized or mitigated. The core takeaway is visibility drives better collaboration and faster problem solving.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A Kanban board visually maps workflow stages and work items, enabling visibility and continuous improvement.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › What is a Kanban board?
Definition

A Kanban board maps stages of work and the items moving through them, enabling visibility and team coordination.

Why it matters
  • Creates a shared view of work and responsibilities.
  • Highlights bottlenecks so the team can act on them.
  • Supports pull-based flow and continuous improvement.
Example
A checkout integration card is moved to Blocked when API keys are missing; that visibility triggers a dependency callout.
Misconception
The board is not a static status report; it must be updated and used to guide pull decisions.
Visual core
Basic board layout
To Do
Items waiting to be pulled.
Card example: "Design product display page"
Doing
Currently worked items where team focus is applied.
Card example: "Create database schema"
Done
Completed work that’s delivered or released.
Card example: "Implement user registration"
Key Takeaway

Visibility is the primary capability a Kanban board provides; use it to spot bottlenecks and coordinate work.

screens.title: Basic board workflow
screens.narratorSegment: The most common starting point is a three-column board: To Do, Doing, Done. The key behavior is pull: team members pull a card into Doing when they are ready and able to work on it, rather than pushing tasks onto someone else. This reduces multitasking and context switching. Each card should represent a single unit of work with a clear title, type (story, task, bug), and an owner. As work progresses, the card moves to Done when acceptance criteria are satisfied. A practical rule you can start with is a work-in-progress limit: set a small maximum number of cards that can be in Doing at any time. For example, if two people can actively work on development at once, the Doing column might be limited to two cards; when that limit is reached, new items remain in To Do until capacity frees up. A common mistake is ignoring WIP limits—without them, teams start too many items and the board no longer reflects true flow. Try pulling one card at a time and notice how throughput and focus change over a week.

keyIdea.title: Pull-based flow
keyIdea.text: Set a small work-in-progress limit and pull cards when capacity exists to maintain flow and focus.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Basic board workflow

To Do → Doing → Done

Practice a pull approach and use a work-in-progress (WIP) limit to protect focus.

Process steps
1
Populate To Do
Add prioritized items with a short title and an owner.
2
Pull into Doing
Pull when you have capacity and follow the WIP limit.
3
Move to Done
Move only when acceptance criteria are met and any tests pass.
Key Takeaway

Pull-based movement and WIP limits keep the board representing real flow and reduce multitasking.

Supporting visuals
WIP limit example
If two developers can work in parallel, set Doing limit to 2. Any additional items stay in To Do.
Common mistake
Adding more people to clear a pile-up instead of addressing the process causing the pile-up.
Try this
Run one sprint week using strict pull and a Doing limit. Observe cycle time and interruptions.

screens.title: Cards and item types
screens.narratorSegment: Cards are the atomic units on a Kanban board. Each card should represent a single unit of work that can be moved independently. Typical card types include user stories, which capture functionality from an end-user perspective; tasks, the smaller work items that make up a story; bugs, which represent defects to be fixed; and epics, which are large efforts broken into multiple cards. On the board, teams often differentiate these types by color, icon, or labels so anyone can understand the nature of work at a glance. For example, in an e-commerce board a 'Implement user registration' card might be a story, while 'Fix payment validation bug' is a bug card with higher urgency. It's helpful to include minimal fields on each card: a short title, the type or label, the owner, and a short acceptance note. A common mistake is packing too much information onto a card; keep each card focused and link to deeper documentation if needed. The practical result is that types and conventions reduce cognitive load and help prioritize work efficiently. Cards and item types means a card is a single unit of work; use types and minimal fields to communicate status and priority at a glance.. In practical terms, user stories, tasks, bugs, and epics — how to represent them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: A card is a single unit of work; use types and minimal fields to communicate status and priority at a glance.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Cards and item types
Card anatomy
  • Title: one-line description of the work.
  • Type/label: story, task, bug, or epic.
  • Owner: the person responsible for moving it forward.
  • Acceptance notes: short criteria for completion.
User story
As a user, I want to log in so I can access my dashboard.
Bug
Payment validation fails when card number length is incorrect.
Visual conventions
Color or icon
Use a color or small icon to mark bugs versus features so they stand out instantly.
Keep cards small
If a card is too large, split it into smaller tasks or an epic and child stories.
Example
Implement user registration = story; Create DB schema = task; Fix login crash = bug.

screens.title: Expanding columns for realistic pipelines
screens.narratorSegment: Real work often requires more precision than three columns provide. Expanding columns clarifies handoffs and creates explicit policies for movement. Common additions include Backlog for potential future work, Ready for items prioritized and prepared to be pulled, In Development which you can break into Development and Code Review, In Testing, Ready for Deployment, and Deployed. An important column to include early is Blocked; any task awaiting external input should sit there so the team sees impediments instantly. For each added column, define a brief policy: for example, 'Code must pass unit tests before moving from In Development to Code Review.' Policies make the board a set of agreements, not a vague status map. Use column names that match your team's language and keep policies visible on the board. In practice, teams evolve columns over time—start small, then add stages only when they solve a concrete confusion or bottleneck. The goal is clarity, not complexity. Expanding columns for realistic pipelines means add only the columns that clarify handoffs and add explicit policies to govern when cards move between those columns.. In practical terms, when to do / doing / done is not enough. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Expanding columns

When To Do / Doing / Done is not enough

Add columns to reflect your real handoffs and make rules explicit so movement is unambiguous.

Example expanded pipeline
Backlog → Ready for Dev → In Development → In Code Review → In Testing → Ready for Deployment → Deployed
Each step corresponds to a clear state and should have a short policy describing required conditions to move forward.
Blocked column
Use this to highlight items waiting on external dependencies so the team notices and acts.
Policy example
"Code must pass all unit tests before moving to Code Review." Write this rule on the board where everyone can see it.
Guidance
  • Start small; expand only to solve confusion.
  • Keep column meanings and policies visible.
  • Use a Blocked column to make impediments actionable.
Try this

Add one column this week and write one policy for it. Observe whether handoffs become clearer.

screens.title: Swimlanes: horizontal organization
screens.narratorSegment: Swimlanes are horizontal rows on a Kanban board that let you visualize parallel flows. They are useful when you need to show different classes of service, different teams, or distinct priority lanes at once. For example, you might create a swimlane for Expedite work that includes urgent customer-facing bugs, another for Standard Features, and a third for Maintenance. Swimlanes make it easy to keep high-priority work visible without mixing it with routine backlog items. They are particularly helpful on a single board that supports multiple streams of work and avoid the need for separate boards. When using swimlanes, clearly define what belongs in each lane — the rule should be simple, such as "Expedite = customer outage issues only." A misconception is that swimlanes automatically prioritize work; they only visualize categories. Prioritization still requires explicit agreement about how to handle items in each lane. For an e-commerce example, place a payment outage bug in the Expedite swimlane so it can leapfrog standard feature work and get immediate attention. Swimlanes: horizontal organization means swimlanes segment the board horizontally to show parallel classes of work or teams while keeping a single source of truth.. In practical terms, use swimlanes to separate types of work, priorities, or teams. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Swimlanes
Swimlanes example

Horizontally divide the board to show different priorities or teams in parallel while keeping all work on one board.

Expedite (top lane)
High-priority, urgent items such as production outages. Rule: only customer outages allowed.
Standard Features (middle lane)
Routine development work delivered in normal cadence.
Maintenance (bottom lane)
Technical debt and small maintenance tasks that are lower priority but still tracked.
Example
A payment outage card in Expedite jumps ahead of a feature card in Standard.
Misconception
Swimlanes don't prioritize automatically; you must define how items are treated across lanes.
Try this
Create an Expedite lane and agree a simple rule for what qualifies before using it for a week.

screens.title: Physical vs. Digital Boards
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between a physical and a digital Kanban board depends on your team's location, need for analytics, and preference for tactile interaction. Physical boards — whiteboards with sticky notes — are excellent for co-located teams because they encourage face-to-face discussion and give a tangible sense of progress. They're simple to set up and very visible in the workspace. However, they don't record history easily and are poor for distributed teams. Digital boards, like Trello or Azure DevOps, support distributed collaboration, store historical data for measuring cycle and lead time, and enable automation such as moving cards when conditions are met. A useful approach is a hybrid: use a physical board for daily team coordination and a digital board to archive work and run reporting. A common pitfall is selecting a digital tool and not maintaining it—if the board becomes stale the team loses trust. Choose the medium that your team will keep current and that meets your reporting needs. Physical vs. Digital Boards means pick the board medium based on co-location, need for analytics, and who will keep it up to date.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Physical vs Digital
Physical board
  • Tactile and highly visible for co-located teams.
  • Encourages face-to-face discussion and quick updates.
  • Limited history and poor for distributed teams.
Example
A team with a co-located room may use sticky notes and a whiteboard for daily standups.
Digital board
  • Works for distributed teams and provides history and analytics.
  • Supports automation, integrations, and reporting on cycle time.
  • Requires discipline to keep current or it becomes stale.
Key Takeaway

Choose the medium your team will maintain and that supports your need for data or face-to-face interaction.

screens.title: Set up a digital Kanban board for an e-commerce project
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough shows how to configure a digital board for a small e-commerce site. Start by creating a board named 'E-commerce Website Project' and add these columns: Backlog, Ready for Development, In Development, In Testing, Ready for Deployment, Done. Next, add sample cards such as 'Implement user registration/login', 'Design product display page', and 'Create database schema for products'. Assign one owner per card and add a label for Priority. Create a 'Blocked' column and a simple 'Priority' label with High, Medium, Low values; mark the registration card as High. If your tool supports labels or fields, add a short acceptance criteria field to each card. screens.title: Spotting and addressing bottlenecks
screens.narratorSegment: A common signal from a Kanban board is a pile-up of cards in one column while upstream columns are relatively empty. This usually indicates a bottleneck in the piled-up stage. For example, if many cards sit in Review while In Progress is quiet, the review step lacks capacity or has unclear criteria. The correct next step is to investigate: look for unclear policies, insufficient reviewers, or blocking dependencies. Options include clarifying the entry criteria for Review, increasing review capacity temporarily, or breaking large review items into smaller parts. A mistake is to flood upstream with more work; that worsens the pile-up. Use data when available: lead time and cycle time metrics can confirm whether the bottleneck is persistent. In a small e-commerce team, a persistent review pile-up might motivate adding a peer-review session or a checklist to speed reviews. The board helps you see where to experiment with changes and measure the effect. Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Spotting bottlenecks
Interpreting pile-ups
A build-up of cards in one column usually means that stage can't process items quickly enough. Investigate capacity, clarity of entry criteria, and external dependencies before changing upstream behavior.
Investigate
Talk with people doing the work, review policies, and check for blockers or unclear criteria.
Intervene
Try temporary capacity shifts, clearer rules, or smaller work items to reduce queue time.
Avoid
Don't push more work upstream; that hides the problem and increases context switching.
Measure
Use cycle time and lead time if available to confirm the bottleneck and to validate improvements.
Assessment prompt
If Review has many cards and In Progress is empty, what does that indicate? It usually means Review is the bottleneck; investigate capacity or rules for review.
Key Takeaway

Use the board to reveal where to experiment and measure changes, not to assign blame.

screens.title: Keeping the board accurate and valuable
screens.narratorSegment: A Kanban board is only valuable if it reflects reality. One common mistake teams make is allowing the board to become stale: cards are not updated, owners aren't assigned, and the board drifts from actual work. This undermines trust and defeats the purpose of visualization. To avoid this, establish a lightweight routine: update cards during daily coordination, mark owners, and record why a card is blocked with a short comment or tag. Another mistake is over-engineering the board with too many columns or rules before the team has a reason to use them. Start simple and add structure only to solve observed confusion. Also, avoid overly large cards; split them so work moves frequently and provides feedback. If using a digital board, periodically archive old cards to keep history manageable. The key is to treat the board as a living artifact: it should guide conversation, not replace it. Regular maintenance and simple policies keep the board trustworthy. Common mistakes
  • Letting cards go stale and not updating status or owners.
  • Over-complicating columns before they solve a problem.

Prevent
Daily lightweight updates and an assigned owner per card keep the board accurate.
Simplify
Start with simple columns and add new stages only when you need clarity on a handoff.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore why a Kanban board is the heart of visual workflow management. A Kanban board turns hidden work into visible work, so everyone on a team shares the same view of what is pending, what is being worked on, and what is done. You will see the basic three-column pattern used widely — and how teams expand those columns, add lanes, and mark different types of cards to match real processes. The board is both a communication tool and a continuous-improvement tool: when you can see where work piles up you can investigate policies or capacity constraints. For example, in a small e-commerce project a single payment integration blocked delivery for days until the team added a 'Blocked' column and an expedite swimlane. A common misconception is that boards are status reports; instead, they are a shared workspace that drives pull-based flow. By the end of this chapter you will be able to design a board for simple and complex workflows and choose between physical and digital approaches that fit your team.

These objectives guide the lesson and focus your practice. First, you will explain the fundamental purpose and benefits of a Kanban board: why visibility matters, how transparency reduces confusion, and how the board supports continuous improvement. Second, you will identify the essential components of a basic board, learning to name columns and cards and describe their roles clearly. Third, you will design an expanded board: adding columns like Ready, In Testing, or Blocked and creating explicit policies for when a card can move. Fourth, you will distinguish physical and digital boards and match each to a team's needs. For each objective, we'll show a mnemonic or small visual to help you remember the skill and a short, practical example tied to an e-commerce project. These objectives are competency-focused: after practicing, you will be able to set up a working board and make simple policy choices that improve team flow.

This second objectives slide gives practical ways to practice and measure each skill. For understanding purpose and benefits, practice by explaining to your team why visibility reduces handoffs and disagreements; use a real example such as how a stuck payment integration became visible. For identifying components, set up a three-column board and explain what each card needs to include: a title, type label, and a responsible person or owner. For designing expanded boards, sketch a pipeline for development that includes Ready, In Development, In Review, and In Testing and then define one explicit policy for moving a card between two stages. For choosing between physical and digital, run a quick checklist on location, need for analytics, and history tracking. Each practice step is short, repeatable, and measurable so you can turn the objective into a competency you can demonstrate to your team.

A Kanban board is a visual management tool that represents your workflow as a series of stages and the work items that move through them. At its core it makes all work visible, turning hidden tasks into tangible cards that anyone can inspect. This visibility reduces miscommunication about ownership and status and helps teams find where flow is obstructed. Think of it as a communal workspace: cards represent units of work such as user stories, bugs, or tasks, and columns represent the stages those items pass through. The key difference from a simple to-do list is the explicit flow — cards move left to right and the team can apply policies about when they may move. A common misconception is that a board is only a status report; in practice a healthy board is a live artifact that teams pull from, negotiate, and update often. As an example, imagine an e-commerce project where checkout integration waits on A P I keys; by placing a card in a 'Blocked' column the team makes that dependency visible so it can be prioritized or mitigated. The core takeaway is visibility drives better collaboration and faster problem solving.

The most common starting point is a three-column board: To Do, Doing, Done. The key behavior is pull: team members pull a card into Doing when they are ready and able to work on it, rather than pushing tasks onto someone else. This reduces multitasking and context switching. Each card should represent a single unit of work with a clear title, type (story, task, bug), and an owner. As work progresses, the card moves to Done when acceptance criteria are satisfied. A practical rule you can start with is a work-in-progress limit: set a small maximum number of cards that can be in Doing at any time. For example, if two people can actively work on development at once, the Doing column might be limited to two cards; when that limit is reached, new items remain in To Do until capacity frees up. A common mistake is ignoring WIP limits—without them, teams start too many items and the board no longer reflects true flow. Try pulling one card at a time and notice how throughput and focus change over a week.

Cards are the atomic units on a Kanban board. Each card should represent a single unit of work that can be moved independently. Typical card types include user stories, which capture functionality from an end-user perspective; tasks, the smaller work items that make up a story; bugs, which represent defects to be fixed; and epics, which are large efforts broken into multiple cards. On the board, teams often differentiate these types by color, icon, or labels so anyone can understand the nature of work at a glance. For example, in an e-commerce board a 'Implement user registration' card might be a story, while 'Fix payment validation bug' is a bug card with higher urgency. It's helpful to include minimal fields on each card: a short title, the type or label, the owner, and a short acceptance note. A common mistake is packing too much information onto a card; keep each card focused and link to deeper documentation if needed. The practical result is that types and conventions reduce cognitive load and help prioritize work efficiently. Cards and item types means a card is a single unit of work; use types and minimal fields to communicate status and priority at a glance.. In practical terms, user stories, tasks, bugs, and epics — how to represent them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Real work often requires more precision than three columns provide. Expanding columns clarifies handoffs and creates explicit policies for movement. Common additions include Backlog for potential future work, Ready for items prioritized and prepared to be pulled, In Development which you can break into Development and Code Review, In Testing, Ready for Deployment, and Deployed. An important column to include early is Blocked; any task awaiting external input should sit there so the team sees impediments instantly. For each added column, define a brief policy: for example, 'Code must pass unit tests before moving from In Development to Code Review.' Policies make the board a set of agreements, not a vague status map. Use column names that match your team's language and keep policies visible on the board. In practice, teams evolve columns over time—start small, then add stages only when they solve a concrete confusion or bottleneck. The goal is clarity, not complexity. Expanding columns for realistic pipelines means add only the columns that clarify handoffs and add explicit policies to govern when cards move between those columns.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Swimlanes are horizontal rows on a Kanban board that let you visualize parallel flows. They are useful when you need to show different classes of service, different teams, or distinct priority lanes at once. For example, you might create a swimlane for Expedite work that includes urgent customer-facing bugs, another for Standard Features, and a third for Maintenance. Swimlanes make it easy to keep high-priority work visible without mixing it with routine backlog items. They are particularly helpful on a single board that supports multiple streams of work and avoid the need for separate boards. When using swimlanes, clearly define what belongs in each lane — the rule should be simple, such as "Expedite = customer outage issues only." A misconception is that swimlanes automatically prioritize work; they only visualize categories. Prioritization still requires explicit agreement about how to handle items in each lane. For an e-commerce example, place a payment outage bug in the Expedite swimlane so it can leapfrog standard feature work and get immediate attention. In practical terms, use swimlanes to separate types of work, priorities, or teams. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing between a physical and a digital Kanban board depends on your team's location, need for analytics, and preference for tactile interaction. Physical boards — whiteboards with sticky notes — are excellent for co-located teams because they encourage face-to-face discussion and give a tangible sense of progress. They're simple to set up and very visible in the workspace. However, they don't record history easily and are poor for distributed teams. Digital boards, like Trello or Azure DevOps, support distributed collaboration, store historical data for measuring cycle and lead time, and enable automation such as moving cards when conditions are met. A useful approach is a hybrid: use a physical board for daily team coordination and a digital board to archive work and run reporting. A common pitfall is selecting a digital tool and not maintaining it—if the board becomes stale the team loses trust. Choose the medium that your team will keep current and that meets your reporting needs. A Kanban board is only valuable if it reflects reality. One common mistake teams make is allowing the board to become stale: cards are not updated, owners aren't assigned, and the board drifts from actual work. This undermines trust and defeats the purpose of visualization. To avoid this, establish a lightweight routine: update cards during daily coordination, mark owners, and record why a card is blocked with a short comment or tag. Another mistake is over-engineering the board with too many columns or rules before the team has a reason to use them. Start simple and add structure only to solve observed confusion. Also, avoid overly large cards; split them so work moves frequently and provides feedback. If using a digital board, periodically archive old cards to keep history manageable.
